state: FreshCart checkout runs with no reserved hosts. ApiEdge takes HTTP checkouts and drops messages on IntakeQueue. IntakeHandler is launched by the cloud vendor only when messages arrive; bursts create hundreds of parallel copies and quiet periods leave nothing running, billed per invocation and per millisecond. It validates payloads and writes to OrderTable. StockSync reacts to table change streams to adjust InventoryStore. NightlyDigest is started by a midnight timer event and runs the same on-demand way, assembling per-tenant sales digests by querying OrderTable, fetching layouts from TemplateStore, and passing MIME text to MailRelay. Each digest query combines tenant id, date window, status list, sort key, limit and projection, with half the clauses conditional on tenant options. Current Python code builds queries two painful ways: nested dict and tuple constructors where outer-inner order hides filter intent, or six to ten setter lines on a QuerySpec temp where reviewers must read every line to see the whole request and misordered assignments slip through. Handlers are kept small, cold-start budget forbids a heavy ORM, and digest code must stay reviewable by data analysts.

state: SeatGrab sells last-minute seats for small venues. Ingress is an HTTPS edge route that emits JSON events. Business work lives in three isolated on-demand handlers hosted on Northwind Cloud on-demand compute: ReserveSeats, ReleaseHold, and PaymentConfirm. Each handler image is uploaded as a zip and the platform starts a copy only when an event or HTTP call arrives, bills for the milliseconds used, and discards the copy afterwards, so no process persists between requests. Shared state is external: a managed key-value Bookings table, a SeatInventory table, and a notification topic feeding EmailFanout. A reserve flow must check seat availability from SeatInventory, validate promo codes, compute total with fees, insert a hold row with TTL, and publish a confirmation, all as one all-or-nothing unit. The team is three backend developers in Python with no appetite for rich object graphs; each screen maps to one write operation and rules rarely change except fee percentages. They need a way to keep each handler's validation, pricing math, and persistence visible top-to-bottom with an explicit commit point, rather than spreading seat rules across interlinked classes.

state: Expensa processes expense receipts without any always-on hosts. EdgeIngress is a managed HTTP front door; POST /receipts invokes IngressFn. Writes to ReceiptBucket (object store) fire OcrExtractFn on each image. A backlog queue ReprocessQueue fires ReplayFn for bulk retries. Each Fn is shipped as an independent zip, instantiated per event with automatic concurrency, billed per millisecond of execution, and reclaimed to nothing when traffic ends, so cold start and package size matter and there is no local affinity between invocations. All three Fns must turn raw OCR text into a minor-units amount before calling LedgerWriter and PolicyStore. That conversion is five small pure unary steps in fixed order: stripWhitespace, fixOcrConfusions, parseDecimal, toMinorUnits, enforceCap. Today each Fn repeats the work as nested calls and copy-pasted temporaries, with slightly divergent order in ReplayFn causing capped values to parse differently. Product wants to add a sixth step for currency canonicalisation and to reuse subsets (first three steps) in a new SlackNotifyFn, plus unit-test each step and the full order, and pass the whole conversion as a single value to a generic retry/timeout wrapper and to an audit logger that records step timings.

state: ShopFast runs device telemetry on Kubernetes. IngestFrontdoor accepts batched POSTs from 800k phones and calls RiskScorer over gRPC for fraud scoring, then LedgerWriter for Postgres inserts. Each Pod runs two containers: the service code and a companion network container. All inbound and outbound calls pass through the companion, which enforces mTLS, applies timeouts and retries pushed from TrafficDirector, and reports traces. IngestFrontdoor sustains 18k events per sec in flash sales, while RiskScorer sustains 5k per sec due to ONNX inference and LedgerWriter sustains 3k per sec due to transactional writes. IngestFrontdoor currently pushes into a limitless in-process queue feeding sender loops. At peak the queue holds over 2M events, memory exceeds the 768Mi Pod limit causing OOM kills and lost purchases, end to end p99 exceeds 9s, and phone retries amplify the surge. Product permits answering 429 with Retry-After for phones to back off and merging repeated GPS pings per device, but purchase events must never vanish silently.

state: Retail checkout runs as five Python services: EdgeGateway, OrderService, FraudCheck, LedgerWriter and NotifyService. Each service runs in Kubernetes as a pod with two containers: the application container and a co-located traffic agent owned by the platform team. Application code never dials another service directly; it sends HTTP to http://localhost:15001/<target> and the local agent adds mTLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing and telemetry before forwarding to the destination pod agent where policy is checked again. A central TrafficDirector pushes routing tables, canary weights and auth policy to all agents, so traffic shifts need no app redeploy. Inside OrderService, OrderProcessor implements checkout business logic. It currently creates its own helpers inside its methods with InventoryClient(), FraudClient(), PostgresOrderStore() and SystemClock(). Supporting sandbox backends in staging or in-memory fakes in unit tests requires editing OrderProcessor, and its required collaborators stay invisible in its API until runtime failures. The release constraints require swapping implementations per environment and verifying logic with fakes without touching business logic, while keeping the full set of required collaborators explicit.

state: Northwind checkout platform runs eight independently deployable Python services on Kubernetes: StorefrontGateway, CartService, PricingService, InventoryService, OrderService, PaymentService, FraudScreen and NotifyService. Each pod runs two containers: a business container with domain logic and a co-located traffic agent injected at deploy time. Business code never dials peers directly; outbound localhost calls are intercepted by the pod-local agent, which applies mutual TLS, load balancing, timeouts, retries, circuit breaking and tracing. OrderService calls PricingService through a PricingClient contract with get_quote(sku, qty). Product now needs optional behaviors around that contract: short-TTL result caching for flash sales, retry with jitter for transient faults, latency histograms, and audit logging. The active set varies by region and feature flag and is chosen at startup from config. PricingClient implementations are generated from IDL and sealed against inheritance, callers hold only the contract type, and creating one subclass per combination would yield sixteen variants plus future growth.

state: NorthStar Insurance runs PolicyAdmin, CustomerDirectory, BillingLedger and ClaimsHandling as independently deployable units owned by separate teams on Java, .NET and Python stacks. Each unit publishes a WSDL contract to a central registry and all cross-unit calls use SOAP over HTTP with XML payloads; the AgentPortal web front end orchestrates them and there is no shared database. To adjust coverage an agent flow is: AgentPortal calls PolicyAdmin.getPolicy and CustomerDirectory.getCustomer to render an edit form for policy P-4412, the agent reviews premiums, beneficiaries and endorsements for 15-30 minutes while taking customer calls, then AgentPortal calls PolicyAdmin.updatePolicy and BillingLedger.reprice. During storm season two agents in different branches routinely open the same policy at the same time. Last quarter three such overlaps caused the second submit to silently erase the first agent's endorsement changes, mispricing premiums. PolicyAdmin uses Oracle and cannot keep a row locked while the agent thinks without blocking ClaimsHandling payouts that read the same rows. Conflicts remain rare and re-entering the form is cheap compared to blocking thousands of reads.

state: NorthStar Mutual runs PolicyAdmin, ClaimSettlement, BillingLedger and CustomerDirectory as separate versioned units deployed on isolated clusters in two data centers. Each unit publishes a WSDL contract and talks to the others only through SOAP over HTTPS with XML payloads validated against shared XSD; a central directory holds endpoint addresses so Java, C# and PHP callers can bind without custom adapters. A new claim flows from ClaimSettlement to PolicyAdmin for a coverage check, then to BillingLedger for reserve posting, then back with status updates. ClaimSettlement keeps its own Oracle store with 42 tables such as CLAIM, COVERAGE_LINE, DEDUCTIBLE and PAYEE. Today every domain class in ClaimSettlement opens JDBC directly: each lists its own columns, converts DATE and NUMBER to Java types, handles nulls and fetches generated keys. The same column lists and conversions repeat across request handlers and batch jobs, and a rename in DEDUCTIBLE forces edits in six classes plus two jobs. The team wants domain logic unit-testable without Oracle, wants one place to adjust column lists and type rules, and wants to add new claim subtypes without copying boilerplate. The question is how to reorganize the persistence code inside ClaimSettlement while keeping its WSDL unchanged for callers.

state: Northwind Traders runs OrderTaker, PaymentSettlement, ShipmentCoordinator and CustomerRegistry as separately deployed processes owned by different teams on Java and C# stacks. Each process publishes a WSDL contract and exchanges XML messages over HTTP with SOAP envelopes routed through a central contract directory with endpoint lookup, so OrderTaker can call PaymentSettlement to authorize totals and ShipmentCoordinator to arrange delivery without shared libraries. PaymentSettlement owns an Oracle schema for invoices and receipts. Each invoice carries a monetary total made of numeric amount plus ISO currency code with rules like non-negative amount and same-currency sums, plus a validity interval with start and end dates used for due checks. Listings and daily sums run at high volume and must complete as single-row fetches with currency filtering in SQL and no extra joins. The schema board forbids new tables for notions that have no lifecycle of their own and are never queried alone. Domain code must still keep amount plus currency as one typed cluster with its checks, not as loose primitives, and the mapper must persist its parts as columns of the invoice row with CHECKs and null handling.

state: FlashSale ticketing platform handles 80k concurrent buyers for stadium tours with no central database on the hot path. Deployment is 4 to 20 identical BookingCell processes on Kubernetes, each holding a 2GB heap-resident partition of seat inventory and price tiers sharded by row hash plus local pricing rules, scaling out by adding cells. Cells stay coherent through a peer replication backbone where every local write is broadcast and merged within 300ms. IntakeGateway shards incoming hold requests by row hash into per-cell intake queues that cells poll, and PaymentWorker and FraudScreen attach as independent consumers. CatalogAuthority is the system of record for venue layouts, price tiers and blackout dates, updated 2-3 times daily by ops. ArchiveLoader snapshots cell heaps to object storage nightly for recovery. Constraint: CatalogAuthority must hand 3-8MB venue datasets to all cells; cells run different code versions and use subsets differently, one checks sightlines, another computes dynamic fees; new consumers must join without changing the publisher; receipt timing must not force immediate action. Direct RPC and shared tables were rejected for coupling and contention.

state: MetroRide runs city surge pricing on a fleet of identical PricingCell replicas. Each cell bundles request-handling code with a RAM-resident partition of zone demand, driver supply and active trip state, kept authoritative in process and flushed asynchronously to Postgres for durability. Capacity is added by starting more cells and repartitioning zones; no central database sits on the hot path. Coordination uses two replicated associative memories, DemandPool and DispatchPool, where cells post and take entries by content matching rather than direct calls, plus a direct peer link between the FareEngine logic in one cell and the DispatchHandler logic in its neighbor for low-latency handoff of trip assignments. In development the pair runs on one host over Unix domain sockets with a custom binary layout; in staging and prod they run across hosts over TCP with TLS, and the roadmap calls for a shared-memory link on roadside units. Today each side hard-codes peer hostnames, socket setup, retries and byte packing, duplicating lookup and framing code. Moving a replica breaks addresses and business logic cannot be exercised without live sockets.

state: NorthStar Fulfillment runs 40 autonomous pick rovers in a warehouse. An edge server hosts Fleet Supervisor which assigns pick missions (aisle, shelf, tote id). Each rover runs a Rover Supervisor on its onboard computer that expands a mission into three side-by-side activities: Navigation Sequencer driving to the aisle, Scanner Sampler pre-warming the barcode camera, and Lift Sequencer preparing forks. Each sequencer in turn calls leaf drivers on microcontrollers: Motor Driver, Lidar Sampler, Gripper Driver, which run 50 Hz control loops and hold exclusive hardware and network leases. Results flow upward: leaf status to sequencers, sequencer summaries to Rover Supervisor, mission outcome to Fleet Supervisor for tote accounting. Constraints: an operator may abort a mission from the dashboard, a Safety Monitor may trip on lidar proximity, or a 30 s mission deadline may expire. On abort the whole nested drive-scan-lift tree must stop promptly, release the gripper safely, close leases, and report aborted distinct from failed, without force-killing threads mid-critical-section or leaving orphaned drive loops burning battery after the caller is gone. Forceful thread kill has previously bent forks and corrupted tote counts.

state: HarborSide fulfillment operates 40 AMRs. Fleet Dispatcher on the edge server assigns transport jobs over a redundant WiFi pub/sub bus. Aboard each vehicle a Unit Supervisor accepts one job and splits it into locomotion and manipulation activities for a Locomotion Manager and an Arm Manager, both ticked at 20 Hz in isolated RTOS partitions. Those managers emit setpoint streams to Wheel Servo Loops and Gripper Servo Loops at 1 kHz on motor firmware and can preempt an activity on obstacle, slip, or low-battery signals. Setpoints flow strictly downward; health and completion signals flow upward; only the servo loops drive hardware. Safety audit requires every motion request queued to the Locomotion Manager to carry a resolved map frame with localization fix, then a velocity and force envelope checked against load, then a live interlock token from the cell monitor, in that exact sequence. Today TraverseOrder is a plain data holder with defaulted fields and independent setters used by routing, tuning, and test tools. Engineers omit the token, swap frame and envelope order, or queue half-filled orders that fail inside the servo loop, far from the mistake. Reviews and runtime checks have not stopped recurrence, and the team wants misuse to be caught by the compiler before an order can reach the queue.

state: HarborSide fulfillment center runs 40 mobile manipulators. Each robot carries an onboard Jetson board hosting three simultaneous loops: a MissionSequencer that steps a pick job through approach, align, grasp, transport and deposit phases and can preempt or suspend the lower loops, a NavigationUnit that consumes lidar and wheel odometry at 20 Hz and outputs velocity commands, and a ManipulationUnit that runs grasp scoring and force-compliant arm motion at 100 Hz. A separate safety board hosts a SafetyGuardian that watches human-proximity lidar and cuts motion output within 50 ms, reporting suspend and resume events upward. A FleetSupervisor on the warehouse edge server assigns jobs, tracks battery and map versions, and pushes route updates over MQTT while robots report phase status and heartbeats upward at 2 Hz. For simulation the team must run identical onboard code against replay logs. Today NavigationUnit builds its own helpers inside its constructor in Python: self.store = LidarMapStore('/maps/site.db'), self.clock = SystemClock(), self.gateway = CanMotorGateway(0x1A). ManipulationUnit similarly builds GraspPlanner(), ForceSensorReader() and the same gateway address. Unit tests needing a fake map, a manual clock or a loopback motor bus must monkey-patch internals or edit the classes, and a reviewer cannot tell what a unit needs without reading its body. Adding a second map backend for the new building would touch every unit.

state: A pharmaceutical distributor monitors 60,000 shipments of temperature-sensitive product. Each shipment carries a data logger reporting every two minutes, and a Go decision service evaluates excursion clauses — allowed range by product class, cumulative time above 8 C, door-open events, seasonal profile — authored by quality assurance staff as versioned sets and published to the service as data, so a stability-profile change never ships a binary. Evaluation is per shipment, but the quality team's questions are spatial and temporal: which shipments were within 200 m of this depot's dock when it lost power; which pallets were in the same cold room between 02:00 and 04:00; which shipments overlapped this truck's route. Today each query scans the whole shipment population — 60,000 live plus 4 million archived — and the incident-response dashboard takes 40 seconds against a 2-second operational target. Positions arrive as latitude and longitude with an accuracy radius every two minutes, and every query is neighbourhood-shaped: a point or a region plus a time window. Constraints: 500 position updates a second, in-memory only for live shipments, archives queryable for seven years, and no change to the clause evaluation itself. Decide how live shipment positions are organised for these queries.

state: A trial sponsor ships site tablets to two hundred investigation sites. Each tablet runs two shells over one behaviour: a PySide6 desktop shell used by site staff, and a browser shell rendered on the same device for monitors who join remotely. The tablets work offline against each site's local trial database and forward entries when a link appears, so the widget cannot call a server for validation. state: A Java ingestion codebase for satellite imagery parses a small language in which operators combine spectral bands with resampling and masking, then evaluates or rewrites the trees across hundreds of scenes. The tree has six node kinds: numeric literal, band reference, binary operator, function call (ndvi, normalisedDifference), resample step and mask step. The binary operator has left and right children, the function call a named argument map, the mask a child plus validity predicate, the resample a child plus output grid. The team must choose how nodes declare children: one base class with a uniform child list, or node classes declaring children in typed fields with their own names, so each pass reads node.left() and node.argument(name) and the type checker cannot confuse a resample's grid with a mask's predicate. Twelve passes run over these trees — band dependency extraction, constant folding, nodata propagation, five rewrites — and operator diagnostics quote a node and a field. Constraints: a 200,000-expression catalogue must parse without the representation doubling memory; a seventh node kind must not force every pass to gain a branch merely to compile; and a diagnostic must name the offending field rather than a positional index.

state: A motor insurer adjudicates claims on two estates: the claim store, document images and the policy master sit in the insurer's own data centre under a data-residency condition, while the adjudication engine, rules service and payment orchestration run in one public cloud region. The claims team is building a behaviour suite for the engine's TypeScript code, which decides whether a claim is payable and at what amount, and calls the on-premises policy lookup through a published client. The existing tests build a claim, call three private helpers to seed the policy and the excess, invoke the decision, then assert on the engine's internal accumulator and on two log lines. A rule change now breaks fourteen tests, and the failures say nothing about which behaviour broke. The team wants every new test to follow one shape: establish exactly the preconditions the behaviour needs, make one call into the engine, then assert the observable outcome the claim handler returns, so a failure names one behaviour. Fixtures must be reusable, and a test must not reach past the published outcome.

state: A contract review platform extracts clause structure from scanned and native agreements. Each document is processed by one stateful remote worker in a Ray cluster: the worker holds that document's parse tables and rule cache in its own memory, receives one call at a time, is addressed by document handle, and is restarted on failure with the document reloaded from object storage. The grammar is a backtracking recursive-descent parser over sixty-two clause rules, with left-recursive corners the authors handle by backtracking rather than rewriting. On deeply nested indemnity schedules it re-derives the same rule at the same input position thousands of times: one hundred-and-eighty-page lease took forty-one minutes and two workers died on memory. The requirement is that no rule is ever evaluated twice at the same position — every rule outcome, success and failure alike, is stored under the pair of rule id and offset before it is returned, and a later visit at that position returns the stored outcome without re-parsing. Caching only successes was tried and the exponential case survived. The cache is per document and dies with the worker. Which design?
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: An agronomy platform predicts irrigation need for 12,000 fields. Soil-moisture probes and weather stations feed a feature service; two models — an evapotranspiration regressor and a seven-day irrigation-need classifier — are retrained weekly on farmer-confirmed irrigation events, validated on a farm-disjoint holdout, registered with their feature definitions, and served by a Go inference service that returns a water-deficit estimate and a recommended irrigation window. The service is assembled as a chain: HTTP handler, scheduler, field enrichment, feature assembly, model run, post-processing — seven stages written by different squads over three years. Every stage takes the request context, but the configuration each needs (model version pin, feature-store endpoint, the tenant's unit system, the irrigation clause profile, a request-scoped trace id and the tenant's water-rights regime) is threaded as explicit parameters from the handler down through stages that never read it. Three of the seven pass six values through untouched, and one stage gained a parameter two years ago that changed 22 call sites. A new tenant-scoped override must now reach the model run, which means editing every signature between. Constraints: 15,000 predictions a minute, a per-request deadline that must propagate, and no shared mutable state across tenants. Decide how the request-scoped configuration travels.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: Brightspan mediates call records for three mobile operators. Four applications, each holding a private database and its own release pipeline: `cdr-intake` (PostgreSQL, on demand, scales on ingest rate), `rating` (PostgreSQL, weekly), `invoice-assembly` (PostgreSQL, daily) and `dispute-ledger` (PostgreSQL, monthly). Each owns its schema; nothing reads another's tables, calls are gRPC, and every application scales on its own metric. The regulator requires that no rating or dispute decision reaches storage without an access decision having been made, and the operators audit that claim. Inside `dispute-ledger` and every other writer, the check must be tamperproof: the code it polices cannot reach it, cannot swap it and cannot skip it. Today the check is a library function imported by each writer, so a new writer can forget it and a compromised crate can replace it. Decide the enforcement point: one small Rust crate compiled as a separate binary that owns a Unix socket and its own memory, with writers holding only a client handle and no linking, and every write routed through it, so the policed code can neither reach nor replace the decision component. Constraints: 40 million records a day, three operators, a five-year audit trail, and a proof obligation that mediation is complete.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: VoltTrace's substation gateway accepts frame submissions synchronously and hands them to a worker tier over a queue. Frames arrive from 900 substation devices speaking three protocol revisions, and about 0.4% cannot be interpreted - truncated payloads, unknown revision, a checksum mismatch, a reading outside the device's declared range. The gateway front and the worker tier are separate; the synchronous side can only note that the frame is suspect. The decision to make: how should a frame that a receiver cannot make sense of be isolated so it can be inspected and replayed later, without stalling the frames that are valid?

state: A roaming settlement venture: thirty charge-point operators and twelve mobility providers settle charging sessions on a permissioned Ethereum network; the operator's node holds the replica and a session is final when the operator and the provider endorse it, and neither can revise it afterwards. The settlement service is Python and its session-posting path takes a ledger client object, posts a session, then reconciles the returned receipt against the operator's own meter record. The team is writing behaviour tests for the reconciliation logic: a receipt whose energy figure disagrees with the meter, a missing endorsement, a receipt that arrives twice. Standing up a real node for these tests is too slow, and a generic stub returns canned receipts the test cannot inspect. The test class itself can implement the small outbound contract the service calls back on, install itself in place of the client, and record the calls and their arguments in its own fields, so the test method asserts on what the service actually asked for. The team must decide how to structure that, including what the test object returns for each case and how it exposes the recorded calls.

state: Beacon Contact runs routing for 8,000 agents across 200 queues. Four applications, each with a private store and its own release cadence: `interaction-router` (PostgreSQL, several deploys a day, scales on call arrival), `agent-state` (PostgreSQL, on demand), `queue-metrics` (TimescaleDB, weekly) and `recording-store` (S3 plus PostgreSQL, monthly). Inside `interaction-router`, an inbound interaction is validated on five points before routing: the calling number is well formed, the dialled number maps to a live queue, the campaign is current, the customer is not on a do-not-call list, and the required skill exists in the queue. Today the validator throws on the first failure, so the console shows one error at a time; a badly configured campaign once took four attempts. Decide how results are reported: every failure found in the pass is collected into a single result object returned to the caller, so all problems are visible at once and the caller decides how to act. Constraints: 2,000 calls a minute, five validation points, a console that must show all failures, and a result that must survive being serialised to the retry queue.

state: A telecom's network service provisioning platform predicts activation failures. Before a service order is dispatched, a model scores the order for the probability that the line will fail physical activation (faulty port, capacity shortfall, address mismatch), and a second model predicts the mean time to activate; the pair is retrained nightly on closed orders, validated on a region-disjoint holdout, and registered with the inventory snapshot they were trained against. Serving is a TypeScript service behind a long-lived internal HTTP API used by three provisioning systems and two field-app builds. The scoring core is being replaced by a vendor's model-runtime SDK whose outputs differ in small ways: score ordering within ties, rounding of the mean-time estimate, the message text of validation errors, and the field order in the response. Nobody can state which of those behaviours the callers depend on — the API has no specification beyond the code, the original author left, and the consumers were written against whatever the service returned in 2022. The team wants to pin the deployed behaviour in committed reference artefacts captured from the live service — request fixtures with their exact recorded responses — so that after the swap a diff shows any behavioural drift before release. Constraints: 40 captured conversations covering the five consumer shapes, artefacts reviewed like code, and a one-week release window. Decide how the swap is made safe.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: Six card issuers, three acquirers and a scheme operator clear authorisation advices on a Besu network with QBFT; nine validators, one per member, and an advice is final only when the issuer and the acquirer endorse it. Each acquirer delivers a settlement advice file every ten minutes containing up to four hundred authorisation records for one merchant batch, and the clearing service, written in Rust against alloy, currently submits the batch as a single transaction. The scheme wants each record carried on its own — its own proposal, its own endorsement, its own retry — while the batch number, acquirer and delivery window travel with every part so the batch can be reassembled for reconciliation and its totals checked. The service must publish a per-batch manifest and reconcile the parts against it. Records for a blocked merchant must be routed to the scheme's exception queue instead of being cleared.

state: A TypeScript construction-procurement codebase issues purchase orders through a third-party supplier client whose interface has five methods. The client comes from a vendor package, callers hold it by concrete class in 60 files, and the cost-control team needs every call to carry the project's cost code, meet a two-second budget, be recorded in the procurement audit trail, and be blocked when a project is frozen. Editing the vendor class is impossible and editing 60 call sites is what the team wants to avoid. The proposal is a wrapper class implementing the same five-method interface (submit, cancel, status, amend, listForProject), taking the vendor client as a constructor argument and intercepting each method: it resolves the cost code from ambient project context, rejects a frozen project, times the call, delegates identical arguments, records request and outcome, then returns or rethrows exactly what the vendor did. Constraints: callers must switch by changing one construction site; the wrapper must not widen, narrow or reorder interface parameters; an exception's type and message must survive; a record must not contain anything the interface did not carry; and a nested call the vendor client makes to itself must not be intercepted twice.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: CityWaste schedules collections for 400,000 households. Four applications, each holding a private store and shipping on its own cadence: `resident-portal` (PostgreSQL, daily, scales on request rate), `route-planning` (PostgreSQL, weekly), `bin-telemetry` (TimescaleDB, on demand) and `billing` (PostgreSQL, monthly). Each owns its schema and scales on its own metric; the portal, the driver app and the back-office console each call the applications they need directly. Three of the four accept a resident or staff cookie, and today each validates it with its own copy of the token check: one reads the role from the cookie, one re-reads it from the database per request, and one honours a renewal the others ignore, so a revoked account kept working on the billing console for a day. Decide where the authenticated session lives: one component mints, validates, renews and revokes it against one Redis cluster, and all three accepting applications call that component and nothing else, so every request is checked against the same policy and a logout or role change revokes access immediately. Constraints: 400,000 residents, three accepting applications, a 15-minute idle timeout, revocation visible within five seconds, and a nightly batch that must not keep sessions alive.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A sports ticketing operator runs one Go binary per venue for seat holds and gate admission. Its interior holds an allocation ledger - hold expiry, seat-to-block mapping, accessible-seat rules, resale limits - and that code imports only the standard library: no SQL driver, no gRPC package, no payment SDK. It depends on four interfaces it defines: SeatMapPort for blocks and holds, PaymentPort for authorising a purchase, TurnstilePort for scanning a ticket at the gate, and AuditPort for the venue's record. Adapters talk to PostgreSQL, a payment processor, the turnstile controllers over Modbus TCP and an append-only audit stream. Gate scanning is the problem: at kick-off, thirty scanners push reads at once, and today each scan calls the ledger synchronously, so a slow audit write holds the scanner's connection and the turnstile queue backs into the concourse. We want each scan and each hold notification reified as a record in a bounded FIFO queue: the scanning adapter enqueues and returns immediately, and one drain loop owned by the ledger takes records in order at whatever rate the ledger can sustain, never interleaving two records for the same seat. Constraints: 1 800 scans a minute at peak, a dropped scan is a legal problem.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A subscription billing service in Rust rates usage records with customer-written rules. Records flow through stages joined by bounded channels: a normalisation stage maps meter names and units, a rating stage applies the compiled rate table, a discount stage applies commitments, and an invoice stage assembles lines. Each stage is its own task on its own thread with its own bounded queue, holds no reference to another, and the discount stage can be reordered after rating per plan without recompiling, which is how annual plans were added. The rate table is compiled from a small rule language that finance writes: tier blocks, per-unit prices, minimum charges, and clauses that reference earlier cost lines. Today that language is read by a hand-written tokenizer feeding a forty-branch state machine, and nobody can tell which production failed. We want the grammar translated rule-for-rule into a tree of functions - each function consumes the tokens its production matches and calls the functions of the productions it references - so the parser's control flow is the grammar, and a failing rule is a named function in the stack. Constraints: 500 rule files, a release per week, byte-offset error messages required by finance, and the compiled output must remain the same stage chain.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A workshop diagnostics product in Kotlin consumes vehicle signals from Engine Control Units. Signals flow through stages joined by bounded channels: one decoder stage per protocol family turns raw CAN and DoIP frames into named signals, a merge stage combines them into a vehicle timeline, a fault stage groups signals into diagnostic trouble codes with freeze frames, and a report stage renders the technician's view. Each stage runs in its own coroutine on a dedicated dispatcher with its own bounded queue and holds no reference to another, so the merge stage can be dropped for a single-bus vehicle and a new protocol decoder is added without editing the rest. The problem is subscription. A dozen source objects each learned about the others, every new consumer had to register with every producer, and two subscribers missed a source last month. We want one hub component that owns the wiring: producers hand it their notifications, subscribers register with it once, and it delivers without the two sides knowing each other, with delivery on the hub's own dispatcher rather than the producer's thread. Constraints: 900 signals a second per vehicle, a subscriber that blocks must not stall decoding, and a late subscriber must be able to receive the current vehicle snapshot.

state: A grocery chain's basket-event pipeline is Java plus Akka: each store's till lane is one long-lived entity holding the lane's open baskets and running totals privately and handling one message at a time; downstream a pricing entity and a stock entity receive derived events. In front of the lane sits an intake point whose mailbox capacity is a configured number, and last quarter two things went wrong. A pricing rollout doubled message volume and the intake grew without limit until the node heap filled at 04:10, taking the store offline. After a cap of fifty thousand was set, a promotion-start burst made the intake block, which back-pressured the till's printer thread and hung a receipt in front of a customer. The team now agrees the capacity must be a stated number and the behaviour at capacity must be an explicit, tested decision rather than an accident: block the sender with a bounded wait, reject with a typed refusal, drop the oldest, fold duplicate scans of one basket, or divert to a separate lane. The choice may differ by message class — sale events cannot be lost, loyalty accruals may be folded, telemetry may be dropped.

state: A hospital group's scheduling platform predicts no-show risk for 1.1 million appointments and proposes overbooking levels per clinic session. Features come from appointment history, referral source, weather and transit disruption; a gradient-boosted model is retrained fortnightly on attended and missed outcomes, validated on a clinic-disjoint holdout, registered with its feature definitions, and served by a Python inference service on FastAPI that returns a risk score and a recommended overbooking count. The service exposes 14 model endpoints: some are internal batch triggers, some clinician-facing, two used by an SMS reminder vendor, and one serves a public patient-facing waiting-time widget. Each endpoint performs its own credential check copied from a shared snippet: three accept a service token in a query string, two skip verification on an internal network, and the copies disagree on whether an expired token is rejected. An external assessment found nine of the 14 reachable by a deactivated staff account. The team wants one checkpoint at the request boundary that decides whether a credential is required for that route, delegates verification to a replaceable mechanism, attaches the resolved subject to request-scoped context, and rejects before any handler runs. Constraints: 20 ms added latency at p99, two identity providers during a merger, and a per-route requirement that must be data, not code. Decide how request authentication is enforced.

state: A streaming platform in Rust issues entitlement tokens to its players. When a subscriber signs in, an entitlement document travels through stages joined by bounded channels: a claims stage gathers plan, territory, device and concurrency facts, a canonicalisation stage normalises the claim set into a byte-exact form, a signing stage signs it with an asymmetric key held in the process, and a publication stage writes the token and the matching verification key to the edge key directory. Each stage runs as its own task on its own thread with its own bounded queue, keeps no reference to another, and the claim stage can be replaced for a partner's entitlement model without touching signing; the profile's stage list is read from configuration at start-up, so a replay-guard stage can be inserted ahead of signing without recompiling. The risk is the signing stage: it is one component that must assemble the issuer's canonical claim profile, apply protected key material that may not be copied to the heap, and publish the matching verification key so a relying party can validate a token without contacting us. Constraints: 90 000 tokens a minute, keys rotated every 12 hours, no claim may appear in a log, and a token must validate offline at the player for 24 hours.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A transmission system operator's outage analytics keeps two computations over one telemetry estate. A periodic full recompute over all retained measurements produces an immutable per-feeder load and interruption view for the year's regulatory filing, and is rewritten from scratch each cycle so no history depends on incremental state. The live feed path holds only present breaker states, protection flags and the last ten minutes of alarms for the control room. The outage API answers a reported fault by merging the rebuilt feeder history with the live alarm window. Inside that API sits the query that hurts: when a fault is reported, the operator needs every sensor within about 500 metres of the reported point, together with its last reading, because the nearest sensors explain whether the fault is upstream or downstream. There are 240,000 sensors, they are read from a fixed-width binary feed in a C# service, and today each reported fault scans all of them, computing a distance per sensor: a storm with 400 simultaneous reports takes the API down. Sensors are re-positioned rarely but re-read constantly. How should they be organised for that query?

The design defines one small contract: a verifier accepts a credential value and returns either a normalised principal — subject id, issuer, assurance level, expiry — or a failure value distinguishing malformed, unknown, revoked and expired credentials. Each mechanism supplies one implementation, and call sites receive verifiers chosen by configuration. Constraints: a mechanism must be replaceable without touching a call site; a verifier must not provision identities or start a login flow; failures must not carry raw credential material into logs; and adding passkeys must not widen the existing four.

state: A university's enrolment platform authenticates applicants, current students and staff from four credential kinds: a password checked against the directory, a SAML assertion from the national federation, a WebAuthn passkey, and a one-time code issued by a partner college. The runtime is a tree of Pykka units with an application-level supervisor: each authentication attempt becomes an isolated unit holding that attempt's nonce, mechanism state and rate counters privately, receiving one message at a time — challenge, response, timeout — and sharing no memory with any other attempt. Verification keys, directory bindings and federation metadata live in separate long-lived units that answer questions; the per-attempt unit asks them by message and cannot read their state. The problem is the return shape: the password path hands back a directory distinguished name, the SAML path an assertion subject, the passkey path a credential id, and four downstream modules compare those with if-chains. The design question is what the boundary should return so every caller gets one normalised principal — a stable person identifier plus assurance level and the mechanism that established it — or an explicit typed failure, with a new mechanism addable without touching login, session issue or audit.

state: A card acquirer's authorization platform evaluates risk and routing clauses on every transaction. It reads and writes only through boundaries it declares: RequisitionPort for the approved requisition, SupplierPort for vendor standing and tax status, CommitmentPort for budget commitments, and AuditPort for the immutable trail procurement law requires. Adapters implement those against the procurement database, the ERP's purchase-order API, the finance ledger and an append-only audit store; the ERP adapter has a contract fixture used in the build. There are sixty use cases and they are all shaped the same way: a single straight-line procedure that loads the requisition, applies the authority matrix and tax rules, writes the order plus its commitments, and finishes inside one database transaction. We are being asked to keep that shape for the next twenty use cases while the authority matrix changes every quarter. Constraints: 500 orders a day, procurement auditors replay any request, and a half-written order must never be visible.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A telecom billing mediation service is written in Kotlin and rates call records as a stream. Records flow through stages joined by bounded channels: a decode stage normalises switch-specific formats, a deduplication stage drops re-transmitted records, a rating stage applies the subscriber's plan, a tax stage adds jurisdiction tax, and a ledger stage writes the charge. Each stage runs in its own coroutine on its own dispatcher with its own queue, holds no reference to another, and the tax stage can be swapped per country without recompiling rating. The rating stage is where it breaks: a subscriber's promotional plan is a tree of rules - bundle applies, then promotional discount, then loyalty tier, which may itself reference another bundle - and the mutually recursive evaluator blows the JVM stack on one in forty thousand records, which aborts the stage. We want each evaluation step to return its next step as a value rather than calling it, with one driver loop in the stage invoking those values until a priced result appears, so depth costs heap instead of stack and the loop can also stop at a deadline. Constraints: 40 million records a night, a depth of up to 4 000 rule nodes, no record may be lost, and the driver loop must be interruptible for a billing freeze.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A subscription billing platform is a .NET service that rates metered usage. Its chain has four stages connected by bounded channels, each on its own thread and unaware of the others: a usage stage normalises meter events into billable quantities, a rating stage applies plan prices, a discount stage adds commitments and credits, and an invoice stage assembles and posts the document. Each stage consumes and produces a value and holds no reference to another, so the discount stage can be removed for a prepaid plan and the rating stage can be run twice over the same usage for a pricing dry run with a different rate card. Rating needs three internal facts about a MeterReading that the usage stage computed - the raw unit count before rounding, the applied conversion factor, and the meter's timezone offset - and those must not become public members of a type that a hundred call sites in this service touch. We are considering a compile-time-only grant: one named sibling assembly holding the rating logic may see those internal members and nothing else, and that assembly exposes one narrow operation that returns the priced quantity the discount stage needs. Constraints: no public surface change in this release, and the rating assembly must be loadable only together with its owner.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A construction procurement platform lets main contractors assemble a bid package from hundreds of small units: each supplier price list, delivery slot, compliance certificate and provisional sum is its own long-lived Thespian process in a system spread over three machines, holding its state privately, reachable only by a registered name, handling one message at a time and restarted by its supervisor after a crash. state: A mail-order pharmacy's refill authorisation service is one Java 21 process. The decision logic - whether a refill is early, whether the prescriber's authorisation still covers it, how many cycles remain, whether a controlled item needs a fresh identity check - sits in a package that imports no Spring, no JDBC and no printer library. That package depends on three boundaries it declares: PrescriptionPort for the prescription and its authorisations, PatientPort for coverage and identity state, and NotifyPort for telling the patient what happened. Adapters back them with PostgreSQL, the benefits clearinghouse's REST API and an SMS gateway; the clearinghouse adapter is a recorded-fixture fake in the logic suite. The package compiles and its tests pass, yet two incidents in a quarter came from call sites that were read wrongly: a method named check() that also consumed an authorisation cycle, a class named Data that held coverage state, a boolean parameter called flag that meant 'prescriber may substitute'. We want the package's types, operations and parameters named after the effect they have in pharmacy vocabulary, so a caller can use them correctly without reading the implementation. Constraints: the regulatory audit needs every state transition explainable in domain terms.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A charging-network operator keeps session history on each site controller, a Go service on the operator's own box in the car park, because the site must show drivers and attendants their recent sessions even when the uplink is saturated by charging telemetry. Head office's console reads that history through the site: an operator filters by connector, date range and tariff, and must page through up to sixty thousand sessions over a slow link without loading them all. Today the read uses LIMIT and OFFSET, and because the site controller appends live sessions and closes others while the operator pages, rows shift under the reader: one operator reconciling a day's revenue saw a session twice and missed another, and offset forty thousand costs the box two seconds per page. The fix must bound each page and carry an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and the ordering, so the next page resumes exactly after the last row the caller saw, sessions added or closed mid-read can neither duplicate nor hide a row, and a token presented with a changed filter is rejected.

state: An airline crew-rostering codebase has three rules sets — cabin, flight deck and standby — that run the same seven-step sequence: load the duty period, normalise local times, check rest and duty limits, score candidate pairings, assign, persist and emit the monthly summary. Today each rules set writes that sequence itself, and the three have already diverged: one persists before it emits, one normalises after scoring, and one skips a rest re-check when a pairing was reassigned. The proposal reverses who drives: a RosterPipeline class owns the sequence once, with run(input) performing the fixed order, and the three rules sets plug in by supplying only the steps that differ — a legality predicate, a scoring function, a persistence hook, a summary renderer — through an abstract class whose default implementations cover normalisation and the rest re-check. Constraints: a hook must not be able to reorder the sequence or skip persistence; an exception in scoring must abort before assignment and leave the previous roster untouched; the summary hook must receive the same immutable result the persistence hook saw; a rules set must be testable by substituting one hook without running the real loader; and existing callers should migrate to one run call instead of a sequence of five.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A TypeScript inventory-replenishment codebase lets a partner-supplied replenishment routine run against live warehouse state during a nightly planning pass. The routine receives four capability objects: a stock reader, an allocation adjuster, an order emitter and a logger; in audit mode the same routine runs with every mutation forbidden. The current guard checks only those four top-level references, so the routine reaches mutations anyway through what it was handed: the stock reader returns records that expose their backing array, the adjuster's callback parameter closes over the mutation API, and a promise resolved with the emitter leaks the unwrapped emitter. The fix under consideration wraps every value that crosses the boundary — arguments going in and objects, callbacks, promises and thrown errors coming back out — with a handler that intercepts property reads, calls and construction, memoised in a WeakMap so cycles terminate and identity comparisons stay consistent. Constraints: instanceof checks inside the routine must keep working, wrapped methods must retain their receiver, and a denied operation must fail with a message naming the capability and the operation rather than a bare type error.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A regional forecasting centre's verification service scores every issued forecast against observations after the fact. The scoring policy is data: verification scientists maintain a clause table — variable, lead-time band, station class, tolerance, score family — as a Git-tracked CSV, and a Rust service compiles it into a package that KusionStack's engine evaluates over each forecast-observation pair, emitting a scored row. About 1.2 million pairs are processed nightly in batches of 50,000. Everything the batch needs is table-shaped: forecast rows, observation rows, station metadata rows and the verdict rows that come out. The service models each as a record struct and keeps the scoring logic in one module with a single instance: methods take a batch of rows, build the facts, run the evaluation across the set, and return a vector of results, with no per-row object retained anywhere. A new requirement strains that shape — bias correction must be computed across the whole set of pairings for a station and applied before scoring, which pushes the module toward caching intermediate aggregates between calls. Constraints: a four-hour nightly window, a 2 GB allocation budget, a clause table that changes monthly, and unit tests that build batches by hand. Decide how the scoring logic is organised against those tables.

state: A construction procurement platform runs as one Spring Boot application: a single jar serving the tender portal, the bid evaluation batch and the supplier registry, with one PostgreSQL database and one release train. The batch and the portal deploy together, and eligibility logic is a plain call inside the same JVM rather than a separate rules tier. Tender eligibility composes small conditions: the bidder must hold a valid licence AND either have completed three comparable projects OR post a performance bond, repeated for each lot, with an exemption list at the end. The current implementation is a 400-line method with nested ifs and three loops, and no rejection reason can be traced back to the condition that produced it. The team wants the rules expressed as a few primitive values plus higher-order combiners - this-then-that, this-or-else-that, repeat-n-times-while, all-of - so an eligibility rule reads as an expression in Java, and every combination carries the trace of which branch decided. Decisions: whether combiners return a boolean or a value carrying reason and trace, how short-circuiting coexists with recording every failed condition for the audit letter, and whether a rule set is rebuilt per tender or resolved once at startup.

state: The same enrolment edge serves a student portal, a registrar console and an automated waitlist worker through one public address, applying authentication, a per-client quota and request signing before any internal call. state: Harbourline Bank's account onboarding runs `onboarding-api`, one FastAPI process in a single container; one deployable, released as a whole. The chain is `router.py` -> `OnboardingService` -> the `Applicant` and `Account` domain classes -> `sqlalchemy_rows`, which owns every statement. state: A fibre wholesaler operates its provisioning platform in Erlang/OTP. Each circuit under construction is its own stateful process holding the order stage, appointment window and line-test results privately; it accepts one command at a time from its mailbox and nothing outside it may read those fields. Around them sit request processes, one per provisioning request arriving from a retailer's API. Three callers drive the same operations: the retailer API, an internal bulk-migration tool and a partner portal. Today each sequences the steps with its own copy of the orchestration, so a change in activation order is made three times and two copies have already diverged. The question is where the published set of provisioning operations should live, and how each operation's coordination and single response should be implemented once for all three callers.

state: A vehicle diagnostics service in Kotlin ingests OBD-II and CAN frames from workshop gateways and produces a session report. Frames flow through stages connected by bounded channels, each stage running in its own coroutine on its own dispatcher: a reader frames the raw bus data, a decoder turns frames into parameter identifiers and diagnostic trouble codes, a correlator groups codes into a fault episode with its freeze-frame, and a reporter writes the workshop-facing report. No stage holds a reference to another or to shared mutable state; each takes a DiagnosticWorkItem, transforms it and passes it on, so the correlator can be replaced with a pass-through for a gateway that already groups codes. Each work item carries a per-item registry of the rows it has loaded from the workshop database, and the rule is that within one item every row is represented by exactly one object: the first stage that needs a calibration record loads it and records it in the registry, and every later stage that asks for the same row by key gets that same instance. Two stages previously loaded the same calibration separately and the report showed two different limits. Constraints: 200 concurrent sessions, three round trips per item, and stages must never share a registry across items.

state: The registrar core is `enrol-core`, one Rust binary (Axum) shipped as a single container image; the chain is handler -> application -> domain -> persistence with no skips. `EnrolHandler` deserialises HTTP and calls only `EnrolmentService`; the service owns the unit of work and calls only the `Course` and `Student` domain types; those types alone call `enrol_rows`, the sqlx module where every statement lives. The course prerequisite graph is loaded once per term and shared read-only across request handlers on a thread pool: each `Prerequisite` owns its children on the heap, and children need a pointer back to the parent for cycle reporting. Today the graph is raw indices into a `Vec`, and a reload while requests are in flight has twice left a dangling index that panicked under load. Decide the reference discipline: a wrapper type that owns the heap value and frees it when the last reference drops, with a non-owning back-pointer for the parent so the graph cannot keep itself alive, versus manual index bookkeeping. Constraints: 40,000 students, a 09:00 term-start burst, 8 GB per pod, `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and reclamation must be observable in the allocator profile.

state: A distribution management system estimates and dispatches feeder state as a stream. Samples flow through stages joined by bounded queues: an ingest stage stamps substation samples with receipt time, an estimation stage solves the feeder's electrical state from its switches and laterals, a constraint stage checks thermal and voltage limits, and a dispatch stage issues control setpoints. Each stage runs on its own thread with its own queue and no in-memory reference to another; the only thing two stages share is the database, where a feeder is stored as a root row whose switches, laterals, regulator taps and protection settings are separate rows. Today the dispatch stage locks each of those rows in turn before writing a setpoint, and the estimation stage locks the same rows in another order, so the two deadlock roughly twice a week and one dispatch was applied to half a feeder. We want one lock covering the whole feeder: taken on the feeder root row, or on a lock entry keyed by that root, or a version token every writer must present. A caller then locks one thing instead of discovering every member, and no two stages can interleave on the same feeder. Constraints: 900 feeders, 5 000 samples a second, lock hold under 40 ms, and no control action may be split across writes.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A cement plant's maintenance system runs on a gateway in the control room, on the plant operator's own hardware, because the corporate CMMS is reachable only through a 2 Mbit satellite link. The gateway holds, per machine, a cluster of dependent records: asset identity and nameplate, sensor baselines and alarm thresholds, open work orders with their labour steps, and the spare-part reservations those orders hold. Today they sit in four tables behind four data-access classes and every screen reloads them separately. A work-order completion that fails halfway leaves the reservation taken and the order open; a baseline update can land while its threshold row is stale. The redesign groups them into one footprint per machine, owned by a single object that loads the whole cluster, enforces its internal consistency (a reservation exists only for an open order; a baseline change forces threshold re-derivation) and saves and forwards the whole graph as one unit of work. When the link comes up the gateway sends each changed footprint upstream as one message, and the corporate CMMS accepts or rejects it whole.

state: CircuitDesk's provisioning service accepts change requests synchronously and enqueues them for a worker tier that talks to network elements. One worker operation - committing a circuit - must only be invocable by the two collaborators entitled to commit, the request worker and the migration tool; today any code that can reach the method can commit, and a maintenance helper did so accidentally last quarter. The team wants the restriction enforced where the call is compiled, not by a runtime check, and they cannot restructure the entitlement because the migration tool lives in another assembly. The decision to make: how should committing a circuit be restricted at compile time to the two entitled collaborators, so any other caller cannot construct the call at all?

state: A Kotlin sports-ticketing codebase has four unrelated types that all need the same three behaviours: a season pass, a single-match ticket, a group booking and a hospitality package must each explain how their price was built, whether they can still be refunded, and whether they can be transferred to another holder. Today the pricing maths is copy-pasted in three of them, and the fourth inherits it from a base class that also drags in an unrelated loyalty field, so a change to the booking-fee rule must be made four times and one copy is already wrong. The proposal defines the behaviours once, outside all four types, in a stand-alone collaborator whose functions take the ticketed item as an explicit parameter: breakdown(ticket), refundableUntil(ticket, now), transferableTo(ticket, holder). Each of the four types supplies a tiny read-only view — face value, event date, transfer count — and owns nothing beyond it. Constraints: no type may gain a common ancestor; the collaborator must be replaceable in tests without touching the four types; the breakdown output must stay stable for 40,000 historical orders; and a new ticket kind must become usable by implementing only the view, never by editing the collaborator.

state: An electric vehicle charging network's back office turns charging sessions into invoices. Sessions flow through stages joined by bounded queues: a start stage records authorisation and the connector, a metering stage appends meter values and detects gaps, a settlement stage applies the tariff and any idle fee, and an invoicing stage writes the document and its tax lines. Each stage runs on its own worker with its own queue, shares no state with the others, and the settlement stage can be replayed over a stored session after a tariff correction, which is how a Dutch price change was fixed. The persistence model is the question. This domain is small - four tables, no inheritance, few invariants beyond a session's monotonic meter values - and each stage today works with a `ChargingSession` class that holds the row's columns as fields, plus the methods that find a session by RFID tag or connector and save it, including the one that marks it settled. A newly hired developer has proposed a separate mapping layer and repository interfaces for all four tables before the next release. Constraints: 1 200 sessions a minute, one deployable, tests that must run without a database container, and the mapped model must not spread across the stage boundary.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: The internal Java toolkit of an industrial machine-maintenance platform is asked to supply one reusable execution helper for the parts-reordering code, the sensor-calibration loader and the warranty-claim sync. All three call code that fails intermittently — a supplier catalogue client, a calibration archive reader and a claims client — and each has grown its own for loop with Thread.sleep; one repeats a non-idempotent submission and another sleeps 30 seconds on a validation failure that can never succeed. The helper is generic over a Callable<T> and a classification predicate: the caller states which exceptions are transient; the helper computes the delay before attempt n as a base interval multiplied by 2^(n-1), caps it at a configured ceiling, multiplies it by a factor drawn from a SplittableRandom in [0.5, 1.5) so callers that failed together do not come back together, and stops on three independent budgets — attempt count, elapsed time and total sleep. Constraints: the sleep budget must be checked before sleeping, not after; a permanent exception must abort without consuming a delay; exhaustion must return the last transient exception with the attempt history attached; and cancellation between attempts must not leave a thread parked in sleep, so the delay must be interruptible.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A flexibility market run by four distribution operators and eleven aggregators settles demand-response commitments on a Besu network; each operator's node holds the replica and a commitment is final when the operator and the aggregator endorse it. The market service is Python and uses web3.py against the local node. Commitments are loaded into memory for the clearing window and passed to a solver that scores them; the solver re-reads the same commitments across three stages, and today the objects it sees are rebuilt between stages, so a commitment edited by an aggregator during the window appears as two distinct entries and is counted twice in the cleared volume. The team wants each commitment object to carry the network's own key for its row, so an instance and its committed row are recognised as the same thing across the stages, across a cache refresh and across a service restart. Object identity is not enough because the objects are deserialised and re-created, and the key must survive serialisation into the solver's input file. Assigning that key is the caller's responsibility; the team must decide where it is attached.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: A fine-art auction house's settlement analytics runs two computations over the same lot data. The completeness path re-runs monthly over the whole bid history in Spark: it recomputes, per lot and per consignor, the complete hammer price, buyer's premium and commission position, and rewrites the immutable settlement partition. Today each of those three callers walks the merged result by index, computing lot order itself, and one of them skips a lot whenever the completeness partition is republished mid-walk, so a consignor statement recently omitted a five-figure lot. Callers must not see how the merged result is assembled or stored, and the ordering must exist in one place. What should hand out the lots?

state: Verifly checks identity documents for 14 markets. Five applications, each with a private store, deployed separately: `document-capture` (S3 plus PostgreSQL, weekly), `liveness-checks` (PostgreSQL, daily), `watchlist-screening` (PostgreSQL, weekly, vendor-fed), `verification-orchestrator` (PostgreSQL, several deploys a day) and `audit-archive` (S3, monthly). Each has its own pipeline and scales separately; nothing shares a schema. Inside `verification-orchestrator`, a verification flow is a configured graph of checks: document type, liveness mode, address check, database lookup, with per-market toggles and timeouts. Fourteen markets produce 40 flow variants, each configured at run time from a JSONB row, and a regulator requires that a March decision can be reproduced with the flow as it stood then. Variants are produced by cloning the flow object today, but the clone is shallow and mutating a variant corrupted the original twice. Decide how new flows are produced: clone a fully configured instance through one cloning operation on the flow type, so creation needs neither the concrete classes nor a repeat of the configuration, and the clone is deep enough that a variant cannot touch the original. Constraints: 40 variants, 90,000 verifications a day, and immutable audit snapshots.

label: security-verification

state: The grid telemetry platform runs as a single TypeScript service on Node: an ingest worker, a query API and the operator report generator all live in one process image, deployed from one container and restarted together. There is one database and one release; the report generator cannot be shipped separately, and an incident fixes all three by rolling the same image back. Operators assemble telemetry queries in the dashboard: pick a substation set, add one or more measurement channels, choose a window, optionally ask for harmonics, optionally for a per-feeder breakdown, optionally for a validated-only filter, and finally request either a JSON envelope or a CSV attachment. The current request object takes fourteen positional constructor arguments, two call sites get the order wrong per month, and mutually exclusive options are caught only when the store rejects the query. The team wants a staged construction object with named, order-independent steps, cross-field rules checked before the request is published, and one terminal call yielding an immutable query. The CSV path needs nearly the same steps but a different final representation. They must decide whether both paths share one staging protocol or the CSV path gets its own, and where the one-time defaults belong.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: VerifyEdge serves mobile identity checks: a phone uploads a document, and one public endpoint authenticates the client, enforces a per-tenant quota and a concurrency limit, and routes to the document service. Inside the document service a shared verification state is guarded by a lock that is acquired in three critical sections. The deployment varies: in the single-node test harness no lock is wanted because the state is thread-confined; on the two-hundred-core batch host a plain mutex serialises every upload and dominates the profile; in the tenant-isolated deployment the state is mostly read and a reader/writer gate is the right choice. The team wants one component that keeps the same critical sections and switches its synchronisation discipline at configuration time, without forking the class or wrapping every section in a conditional. The decision to make: how should the document service parameterise its synchronisation so the same critical sections can run unsynchronised, mutex-protected or reader/writer-protected per deployment, without editing them?
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: Nine hundred pharmacies, three wholesalers and a medicines regulator track batch movements on a shared network where a batch's history is authoritative only after the manufacturer and two wholesalers endorse it. When the regulator issues a recall, the system walks from the recalled batch through every downstream dispensation and builds the list of affected patients and stock locations. The traversal is generated from a seed: batch, then the dispensations that consumed it, then the patients and stock transfers that consumed those, four levels deep, and the resulting tree is immediately reduced to a flat set of notifications and stock flags. Today the code materialises the whole expansion into an intermediate tree and then folds it, and on the largest recall last spring the tree held 2.1 million nodes and the service exhausted its heap. The team wants one recursive walk that expands each seed and consumes it as it goes, so no intermediate tree is allocated and the reduction runs directly over the expansion. Depth limits, cycle detection through transfer chains and the notification payload must survive unchanged.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: Eleven hundred pharmacies, six wholesalers and a regulator record controlled-substance dispensation on one permissioned network; five participants must endorse a dispensation before it is final, and no participant's operator can alter an entry once committed. Each pharmacy runs a dispensing application from one of three vendors plus an integration assembly that submits and queries prescriptions. The lead wants the calling contract alone in its own deployment unit: the application compiles against the interface package only, the implementation is resolved at run time from whatever the pharmacy installed, and a missing or incompatible implementation fails at start-up with a clear message rather than at the first prescription.

state: A speciality insurer's underwriting engine runs on protoactor-go: one long-lived worker per submitted risk across a three-node cluster, addressed by risk reference, with the case's exposures, referred limits, authority tier and outstanding referrals held privately in that worker and changed only by messages it handles one at a time. state: A Rust library that books and settles securities trades currently represents a trade as one struct with a status field, and every operation checks that field at run time: matching an already-cleared trade, settling an unmatched one and cancelling a settled one all compile and fail later with a SettlementError. Two incidents in a quarter came from a caller that ignored such an error. The proposed shape moves the stage into the type: a shared core holds instrument identifier, quantity, counterparty and trade date, a zero-sized type parameter marks the stage, Trade<Draft> exposes only submit, submit yields Trade<Matched>, only Trade<Cleared> has settle, and a cancelled stage carries the reason as a payload. Persistence hands back rows from a table with a status column, so a reconstitute function must branch on the stored string and rebuild the matching stage. Constraints: no field may be declared twice across stages; a stage marker must cost nothing at run time; reconciling 200,000 stored rows must not allocate an intermediate representation per row; and the settlement report, which walks every trade, must keep working through one common trait.

state: A C# warehouse-robotics codebase models a conveyor layout as segments — straight runs, curves, switches, merge points, transfer tables — and the layout importer must turn a configuration file's kind strings into the right segment objects. The importer was a fourteen-branch switch, and every new segment kind from the mechanical team meant editing that switch in the same change as the new class, which produced two merge conflicts a month and one branch that silently imported a switch as a straight run. The proposal inverts the dependency: the importer owns an empty table of named construction functions, and each segment kind contributes its own entry — ("switch", spec => new SwitchSegment(spec.Id, spec.Inlet, spec.Outlet, spec.Failsafe)) — from the file where the kind is defined, so the importer never names a segment class. Constraints: a duplicate kind name must fail loudly when the table is filled; an unknown kind in a file must produce an error naming the file position instead of a skipped row; the table must be populated without reflection because the build ships trimmed; a construction function must be able to reject a spec with a validation error the importer reports with file position; and tests must be able to run the importer with a table containing a fake kind.
instructions: Which design-pattern category does this decision belong to?

state: An EV charging operator's session service is one Kotlin deployment: a single Ktor application in one JVM that terminates charger connections, meters energy, and bills sessions against one PostgreSQL database. It ships as one artifact and the whole process restarts together; the meter loop and the billing API are the same release, and no per-charger process exists to scale separately. Each of 30,000 chargers has mutable state - connector status, meter readings, an active session, a reservation - and today that state lives in a concurrent map guarded by per-charger locks. Two code paths still mutate a session from the websocket thread and the billing thread at once, which produced fourteen double-billed sessions last month. The team wants each charger's state owned by exactly one cell: a small object with its own mailbox and a coroutine that takes one message per turn and returns a reply. Everything else reaches that state only by posting a message and awaiting the response; nothing shares the mutable object, so no locks are needed. Every cell lives in the same process and is rebuilt from the database on start-up. Decisions: whether mailboxes are bounded and what happens when full, and whether one cell may post to another.
